findings.caveat: The 2024 judgment assessed the situation on 28 March 2020. Some professional guidelines existed; the finding concerns incomplete coverage. findings.title: Posted workers: two new expense items missing from the national list
findings.euChange: The amendment added host-state accommodation conditions and reimbursement for professional journeys within the posting assignment to Article 3(1). It requires equal treatment where host-state entitlements exist, not universal employer-provided accommodation.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Slovenia’s core list for workers posted into the country leaves out accommodation and expenses, which the EU now requires to be treated equally where local workers have such entitlements. Other laws, collective agreements and practice were not fully audited, and we do not claim that posted workers lack these rights.
findings.nationalGap: The Commission identified inbound coverage gaps. findings.caveat: This is a scoped list omission and Commission concern, not a court finding. Other laws, collective agreements and practice were not fully audited. Longer postings receive broader rights after 12 months (18 after a motivated extension) under Article 210(6)–(7). No claim is made that every posted worker lacks these rights.

findings.title: Environmental information: old wording kept after an EU correction
findings.statusLabel: Text divergence · legal effect qualified
findings.statusDetail: Official guidance applies the EU definition
findings.summary: In 2022 the EU corrected the Danish text of its definition of environmental information. Denmark’s statute still uses the earlier words, but official guidance tells authorities to apply the EU definition.
findings.euChange: Article 2(1)(b) and (c) changed from factors or measures that affect or can affect the environment to those that affect or are likely to affect it.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. The Danish statute still defines environmental information with “can affect” where the corrected EU text says “are likely to affect”. This does not show that anyone’s access to information was reduced: official guidance applies the EU definition, and EU law permits wider national access.

findings.resolution: A 2025 ministry report says the EU definition must govern despite the difference in words. The Ombudsman’s guide also points out the correction.
findings.caveat: A documented textual divergence, not an established breach or finding that access rights were reduced. Recital 24 permits wider national access. Conforming interpretation and the actual breadth of access require separate analysis. The corrigendum sets no fresh transposition deadline.

findings.title: Jam: national decree lagged behind the EU’s higher fruit minimums
findings.statusLabel: Government-admitted delay · October 2026 concern
findings.statusDetail: The government admitted the delay
findings.summary: Belgium has admitted that its jam decree is late. In October 2026 the Commission reported that Belgium had not fully notified its measures.
findings.euChange: Article 3(4) and Annex II(1)(a) raised the general fruit-content minimum per 1,000 g of finished ordinary jam from 350 g to 450 g, and extra jam from 450 g to 500 g. Specific fruits have separate thresholds. Article 5 required national adoption/publication by 14 December 2025 and application from 14 June 2026.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Belgium’s 2004 rules set the old minimums (350 g of fruit per kg of ordinary jam, 450 g for extra jam). Belgium has admitted that its replacement is late and it was still forthcoming in July 2026; we have not treated the draft as enacted. Jam placed on the market or labelled before 14 June 2026 may still be sold until stocks run out, and the Commission’s opinion is an allegation of incomplete notification, not a judgment.
findings.nationalGap: The 2004 decree used general minima of 350 g/kg for ordinary jam and 450 g/kg for extra jam. The Economy Ministry said its replacement remained forthcoming on 3 June 2026; a written ministerial answer on 8 July confirmed a delay involving national fruit-spread rules and the EU technical-notification process.
findings.nationalLaw: Royal Decree 19 March 2004 on manufacture and marketing of jams, jellies, fruit marmalades, chestnut purée and fruit spreads, Article 1§2; replacement decree pending in the government’s July 2026 account.
findings.provisions: Directive 2024/1438 Article 3(4), Annex II(1)(a), Articles 5–6; Belgian 2004 decree Article 1§2(1)(a),(2)(a).
findings.resolution: An official EU notification draft (TRIS) contains the new minimums. On 1 October 2026 the Commission sent a reasoned opinion saying no measures had been notified for the jam rules. We found no enacted replacement; lack of notification alone does not prove that no law exists.
findings.caveat: The government’s June/July statements establish a historical legislative delay. The October 2026 Commission reasoned opinion is an allegation about incomplete notification, not a judgment or conclusive evidence of continued legislative absence. No claim is made that every jam sold is non-compliant: Article 6 allows products placed on the market or labelled before 14 June 2026 to be sold until stocks are exhausted. Special-fruit thresholds also differ. The draft is not treated as enacted law.

findings.title: Waste prevention: wording replaced by the EU in 2018 is still in use
findings.statusLabel: Current text lag · correction remains a draft
findings.statusDetail: Ministry draft; Cabinet proposal aimed for January 2027
findings.summary: Germany still uses the earlier terminology in its definition of waste prevention (“harmful” instead of “hazardous” substances). The environment ministry has a draft that would update it.
findings.euChange: Article 1(3)(e) replaced Article 3(12)(c) of the Waste Framework Directive: the prevention definition now refers to reducing hazardous substances in materials and products, replacing harmful substances.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. German law says “harmful” substances where the EU text now says “hazardous”. “Harmful” may be the broader word, no practical difference in scope has been established, and the ministry’s draft would update the wording.
findings.nationalGap: KrWG Section 3(20) retains schädlichen Stoffen. The ministry proposes gefährlichen Stoffen, expressly linking the replacement to the 2018 amendment.
findings.nationalLaw: Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz (KrWG), Section 3(20), sentence 1; draft amendment Article 1(4)(c).
findings.provisions: Directive 2018/851 Article 1(3)(e), replacing Directive 2008/98 Article 3(12)(c); Article 2(1) transposition deadline.
findings.resolution: The ministry’s webpage, updated 30 September 2026, lists the proposal as a draft still in progress and aims for a revised Cabinet proposal in January 2027. The official national text, checked on 25 October 2026, still has the earlier wording.
findings.caveat: This establishes an acknowledged textual update lag, not reduced environmental protection or harm. Harmful may be broader than hazardous; no practical scope difference was established. The draft is not enacted law. This wording is not specifically identified in the public Commission statement for the separate waste infringement case INFR(2025)2047. The draft’s 2027 timetable does not extend the old 2020 transposition deadline.

findings.title: Hazardous waste: an economic exception the EU removed is still in national law
findings.statusLabel: Current national exception · correction remains a draft
findings.statusDetail: Ministry draft would delete the exception
findings.evidenceLabel: National text checked
findings.summary: Germany still lets companies skip separating illegally mixed hazardous waste if separation is economically unreasonable. The ministry proposes deleting this exception.
findings.euChange: Article 1(16) replaced Article 18(3). Unlawfully mixed hazardous waste must be separated where technically feasible and necessary for Article 13 environmental and health protection. The earlier EU text expressly mentioned economic feasibility; the replacement omits that qualification.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. German law still lets operators skip separating unlawfully mixed hazardous waste when that is economically unreasonable, which the revised EU rule no longer mentions. This concerns only unlawfully mixed hazardous waste, not ordinary household waste, and the ministry itself proposes deleting the exception. Whether any operator used it, or any harm resulted, was not checked.
findings.nationalGap: Current KrWG Section 9a(3), sentence 2, permits transfer to an authorized treatment facility when separation is economically unreasonable. The ministry proposes deleting that exception as incompatible with the revised EU rule.

The ministry’s incompatibility assessment is not a court judgment. A proposed deletion is not an enacted fix.

findings.summary: Irish Regulation 6(4) still treats solid biomass used in plants below 20 MW as meeting the sustainability criteria. The EU threshold has fallen to 7.5 MW, and the official amendment register shows no change to the Irish rule.
findings.euChange: Solid-biomass criteria start at 7.5 MW.
findings.nationalGap: S.I.350/2022 Regulation 6(4) deems solid biomass fuels used in installations with total rated thermal input below 20 MW to fulfil the sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria. Regulation 6(10) limits financial-support eligibility to compliant fuels; Regulation 8 establishes SEAI's verification procedure by reference to Regulation 6. The official amendment register records many later changes to S.I.350/2022 but none to Regulation 6 or Schedule 3. This leaves the express automatic-compliance provision covering the 7.5–less-than-20 MW band newly covered by the EU amendment.
findings.nationalLaw: European Union (Renewable Energy) Regulations (2) 2022, S.I.350/2022, Regulations 6(4), 6(10) and 8; official chronological amendment table updated to 13 October 2026.
findings.provisions: RED III Articles 1(19)(a)(iii), 5(1); RED Article 29(1),(15); national Regulation 6(4).
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Ireland’s automatic exemption covers plants between 7.5 and 20 MW that the EU now includes. Whether any subsidy decision, fuel delivery or miscounted plant has been affected has not been established.
findings.resolution: We found no Irish law changing Regulation 6(4) and no official acknowledgment of this mismatch. The SEAI verification page still points operators to S.I. 350/2022 and the RED II criteria. A separate SEAI report had already described the EU threshold falling to 7.5 MW in 2025; that shows awareness of the EU change, not an admission that Irish law omitted it.
findings.caveat: This is a statutory-text lead. The criteria govern renewable-energy accounting, obligations and support, rather than general permission to burn biomass. Article 29(15) preserves old criteria until 31 December 2030 for qualifying support granted before 20 November 2023, with fixed long-term amounts and an anti-overcompensation mechanism; focus on installations outside that route. Separate scheme conditions, EU ETS requirements and verification practice need further review. The official amendment register stops 13 October 2026; targeted later-enactment searches found no correction.

comparison.before: Solid biomass used below 20 MW counts as meeting the sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria automatically.
comparison.after: The criteria apply from 7.5 MW (with exceptions).
comparison.note: Focus on the 7.5–less-than-20 MW band outside qualifying pre-November-2023 support.

findings.review: Two agents independently checked the authentic EU amendment, original Irish regulation, official amendment table updated to 13 October 2026, the listed 2025–26 amendments and current SEAI verification instructions. Both checked Article 29(15) grandfathering and searched for standalone overriding legislation. No contrary threshold amendment located; actual scheme conditions and individual installations remain unverified.

findings.summary: A 2026 EU amendment allows three specific uses of cobalt in toys. Hungary’s list of permitted substances still names only nickel. A government draft published in October proposes adding cobalt, after the EU’s implementation dates.

Directive-consistent interpretation and EU free-movement rights may protect compliant products despite the national text. No claim of unsafe toys, actual trade obstruction or deliberate disregard is made. The new Toy Safety Regulation does not fully replace these rules until 2030.

findings.nationalGap: Article 135a(8)(2) applies the sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria to solid biomass used in installations commissioned after 31 December 2020 with total rated thermal input of at least 20 MW. Article 129(5) uses that same installation definition for renewable-energy accounting, and Article 135b links it to certification. The official consolidated text dated 3 August 2026 retains the threshold. The original act’s amendment metadata, updated 16 October, lists only one later amendment: Act 4 September 2026, Dz.U.1347. Its final text does not amend Article 135a, proceeding from changes to Article 124a to Article 136. Government project UC118 remains distinct and expressly proposes the lower threshold.

findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Poland’s threshold leaves plants between 7.5 and 20 MW outside these statutory checks. Whether any fuel delivery, accounting decision or subsidy payment has been affected has not been established.

findings.summary: French Consumer Code Article L217-13 still adds six months to the legal guarantee after a repair, where the EU now requires twelve. The government’s September explanation says the increase to one year awaits transposition.

findings.nationalGap: Article L217-13 continues to provide a six-month extension for goods repaired under the conformity warranty. The current official article, checked with a 25 October 2026 version header, has not been replaced with twelve months. findings.title: Energy sharing: collective rules still require a legal entity
findings.statusLabel: Current framework difference · legal review needed
findings.evidenceLabel: Live current statutory and regulatory provisions checked
findings.summary: France’s framework for collective self-consumption still links participants through a legal entity. We found no equivalent route without one. Ordinary authorised direct electricity sales are already possible, which is an important qualification.
findings.euChange: Article 15a(2) adds the private-agreement alternative.
findings.nationalGap: Energy Code L315-2 requires producers and consumers in ordinary and extended collective self-consumption operations to be linked within a legal person. D315-9, rewritten in June 2026 and effective 1 July, still requires that person to contract with the distribution-system operator. The current framework therefore retains the organisational requirement rather than expressly providing the private-agreement alternative. The 2026 allocation reforms do not remove it.
findings.nationalLaw: Energy Code L315-2 and D315-9; direct-sale alternative L333-1(I)(2).
findings.provisions: Amending Article 2(5); revised Article 15a(2), (4); Article 3(1). National L315-2, D315-9, L333-1.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. The collective-sharing route we identified still requires an organising legal entity. This does not show a general ban on private electricity transactions, a refused project or quantified harm.
findings.resolution: We read the current provisions L315-2 and D315-9 on 25 October 2026. Searches of later legislation and official sources found no separate sharing framework without a legal entity. The Commission’s September 2026 procedure concerns incomplete implementation of energy sharing and supplier choice more broadly; it does not prove this specific difference.
findings.caveat: L333-1(I)(2) permits direct private sales where the producer has supplier authorisation or delegates the obligations to an authorised third party. Such a sale is not automatically equivalent to energy sharing with metered deduction and the small-household supplier exemption in Article 15a(4). Existing collective projects remain possible; geographic limits, balancing responsibilities and charges may lawfully apply. This is a qualified framework comparison requiring legal assessment, not an adjudicated infringement.

findings.baseAct: Dutch civil jurisdiction rules; Directive 2024/1069 creates new EU safeguards
findings.statusLabel: Contested implementation · current jurisdiction wording

findings.summary: The July implementation act added security and full costs, but no separate home-court forum for targets of abusive lawsuits brought outside the EU. General Dutch jurisdiction can already cover many cases; whether its extra connection requirements leave gaps is disputed.
findings.euChange: Article 17(1) creates a domicile forum for third-country SLAPP compensation.
findings.nationalGap: Current Rv 6(e) links tort jurisdiction to the harmful event in the Netherlands. Pure financial loss requires additional connecting circumstances. The July act left Article 6 unchanged. A proposed new 6(j) addressing this difference was withdrawn. The Ministry maintains that existing jurisdiction already suffices; the Amsterdam court and parliamentary amendment explanation identify a distinct EU domicile-based forum.
findings.nationalLaw: Wetboek van Burgerlijke Rechtsvordering Articles 1, 6(e), 9; Act 8 July 2026, Stb.185, effective 14 July.
findings.provisions: Directive 2024/1069 Articles 17(1),(2),18,22(1); Rv 6(e),9; Stb.2026/185 Article I; proposed amendment 36731-11.
findings.consequence: Possibly. In some financial-loss cases the Dutch forum still depends on connections beyond the target’s domicile. The government considers existing law sufficient, and the Amsterdam court accepted jurisdiction in an older case under existing law, so this is a contested assessment of coverage, not a finding that Dutch targets lack a court.
findings.resolution: The current code version, running from 14 July 2026 to the research date, has no Article 6(j). The July implementation notice still relies on Articles 1 and 6(e). We found no later statutory remedy.
findings.caveat: The government considers existing law sufficient: public participation from a Dutch home or reputational loss there may establish jurisdiction. Article 9 supplies exceptional fallback grounds. Conforming interpretation may assist future cases. The Amsterdam court accepted jurisdiction in Greenpeace’s case under existing law; its foreign proceedings began in 2017/2019, so the directive was not applicable there. That judgment did not decide every future post-directive case. Pre-existing international agreements remain protected by EU Article 18. The January 2026 Dutch costs corrigendum is a separate issue and is not the alleged source of this jurisdiction gap.
